transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess the main thing is my eating at night. Most nights after my wife goes to bed, I end up in the kitchen and it’s like I’m eating way past a normal plate of food. Like, fried chicken, mac and cheese, sweet potatoes, rolls—if we had some event or family thing, whatever leftovers are there.

And I’ll just keep going until… I don’t know, sometimes a whole tray is gone, or it feels like half the fridge. It sounds ridiculous saying it out loud. I used to joke that I just like late-night snacks, like when we’d stay up in college and order food, but this isn’t really that. It’s more like I get started and then suddenly there’s just a lot missing.
When you're eating like this at night, do you feel like you can’t stop or control how much you’re eating?

Yeah… yeah, that’s pretty much it. Like once I take that first bite, it feels like the decision’s already been made for me. I’ll be standing there thinking, George, stop now, you don’t need more, and then somehow my hands are still making another plate or opening another container.

It’s weird because it’s not like I’m confused, you know? I know what I’m doing. It’s just… I don’t feel like I can turn it off once it starts.
Does this nighttime eating cause you a lot of stress or interfere with your daily life, like affecting your relationships or how you feel about yourself?

Yeah… it does. More than I like to admit, probably.

I used to be pretty involved with, like, community planning stuff—meetings, helping set up events, making sure tables were where they needed to be, all that. I mean, I was never the mayor or anything, but people knew they could ask me to pitch in. Lately I’ve just… pulled back from all of that.

Part of it is I feel embarrassed, like people can tell I’m not really holding things together the way I used to. And I’m drained, too. Even just showing up and making small talk feels like a lot. So yeah, it’s not just eating and then forgetting about it. It kind of follows me around.
Do you ever wake up during the night feeling like you're not fully asleep and find yourself eating without really being aware of it, or do you feel unusually sleepy during the day?

Um… I don’t know that I’d say I’m not aware of it. I mean, I’m awake enough to know I’m in the kitchen, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like sleepwalking or waking up with wrappers and no memory.

The daytime sleepy part… I mean, I get tired, but who doesn’t, right? My uncle used to fall asleep in his recliner every Sunday with the football game on, and everybody acted like that was normal. So I don’t really know where the line is. I haven’t noticed anything like… unusual, I guess.
Lately, have you noticed feeling down or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, like the community events you mentioned stepping back from?

I mean… I don’t know. “Down” is kind of a big word, right? Like, everybody has days where they don’t want to deal with people.

The community stuff… yeah, I haven’t been going much, but part of that is just—well, those meetings can drag on forever. There was this one guy who’d argue for twenty minutes about where to put a trash can, and I’d sit there thinking, how is this my evening? So maybe I lost patience more than interest.

I guess I’m not totally sure what counts as losing interest versus just not feeling up for it lately.
Over the past few weeks, have you found yourself feeling down or depressed most of the day, more days than not?

I’m… not sure I’d put it that way. Like, most of the day, more days than not—that sounds very official, and I don’t really track it like that.

Some days I’m just in a mood, or I don’t want to talk to anybody, but then I’ll get distracted by something stupid, like trying to fix the cabinet hinge in my kitchen for an hour even though I don’t know what I’m doing. So I don’t know if that counts as depressed or just… being off.

I guess I haven’t really noticed it in that clear of a pattern.
Can you think of a recent day when you felt down or low for most of the day, and if so, how often has that happened in the past few weeks?

I’m trying to think of one, but it’s hard to pin down. Like, I can remember days where I woke up already kind of annoyed or heavy, if that makes sense, but then the day gets chopped up by random stuff—phone calls, dishes, some YouTube thing I didn’t mean to watch for two hours.

So I don’t know if I’d say “most of the day.” I don’t really keep track that way. Past few weeks… maybe a few off days? But I couldn’t honestly tell you how often without guessing.
Can you recall if there were any days in the past two weeks where you felt down or low for most of the day, and if so, how many days would you say that happened?

I honestly don’t know. Two weeks sounds short, but when I try to look back it all kind of blurs together.

Like, I can remember being low in bits—standing in the kitchen or sitting on the couch and not wanting to move—but then I’ll get pulled into something else, or I’ll start messing with my phone, and suddenly it’s nighttime. So I don’t know if that means it was most of the day.

If I had to give you a number, I’d just be guessing. Maybe there were some days, but I can’t say how many.
Have you had any days in the past week where you felt down or low for most of the day, and if so, how many days would you say that was?

Past week… I don’t really know. I know that’s probably not helpful.

There were moments where I felt low, like sitting there and realizing I’d been staring at the same thing for a while, but then I’d get distracted by some random errand or I’d start reorganizing something I didn’t need to reorganize. Like I found myself sorting old cables in a drawer the other day, and I don’t even know why I kept half of them.

So… days where it was most of the day? I can’t really say. I haven’t been keeping track that cleanly.
Do you ever feel so distressed about this nighttime eating that it interferes with your ability to function at work, at home, or in social situations?

Yeah… yeah, I think it does. Not like I can’t get out of bed or anything, but it sort of messes with how I show up.

I used to be more involved with community planning meetings and helping set up events—like neighborhood stuff, little committees, things like that. And lately I’ve pulled back from a lot of it. Part of it is I’m embarrassed, I guess. I feel drained, and I worry people can tell I’m not really keeping things together like I used to.

It’s weird, because those meetings aren’t even that dramatic—half the time it’s just arguing about folding chairs or who forgot to print flyers—but I’ll avoid going because I don’t want to be seen that way. So yeah, it has interfered some.

Can you tell me more about how your nighttime eating specifically affects your ability to participate in social or community activities, and if you've noticed it impacting any other areas of your life like work or family responsibilities?

Yeah… it mostly shows up with the community stuff. I used to go to those planning meetings and help with little events, and now I just kind of… don’t. I’ll tell myself I’m tired or that they have enough people, but really I feel embarrassed.

After nights where I’ve eaten like that, I wake up feeling drained, and then I’m already thinking, “People are going to notice something’s off with me.” Like I’m not holding it together the way I used to.

And it’s not like those meetings are life-or-death. Sometimes they’re just talking about tables or permits or who’s bringing coffee, and somehow even that feels like too much. I start avoiding them. As far as work… I’m not working right now, so I can’t really say there. Family stuff, I don’t know, not as clearly. The community things are where I notice it the most.
Do you feel a lot of guilt, shame, or self-criticism specifically about the way you eat at night, even aside from how it affects your daily activities?

Yeah… yes. That part is probably worse than the tiredness, honestly.

After it happens, I just feel… sick with myself. Like, I’m sitting there thinking, “What is wrong with me?” And then I’ll think about how people see me—or how I want them to see me, I guess—as someone organized, dependable, strong. The guy who can handle things, who keeps the meeting notes straight, who knows where the extra extension cords are… and then there I am, alone at night, ashamed and guilty and disgusted that I let it happen again.

It’s not just “oh, I ate too much.” It feels like I failed at being the person I’m supposed to be.
When you’re eating at night, do you ever feel like you’re only partly awake, or like you’re on autopilot, not fully in control of what you’re doing?

I don’t know if I’d say I’m half-asleep exactly. It’s more like… once I take that first bite, something clicks over, and then it feels like the decision’s already been made for me.

I can be standing there thinking, George, stop. Just stop now. And meanwhile my hands are still doing it—fixing another plate, opening another container, putting something else together like I’m just following instructions. It’s a strange feeling.

It reminds me of when you drive somewhere familiar and realize you don’t remember half the turns you made—not that it’s the same thing, but that kind of autopilot. Except with this, I’m aware enough to feel ashamed while it’s happening, which makes it worse.
Has your nighttime eating caused any problems in your personal relationships, or do you find yourself avoiding certain situations with your family or friends because of it?

Yeah… I guess it’s less with family directly and more that I’ve started avoiding people in general, especially the community planning stuff. Like, I used to show up and help with events, make calls, organize little things—nothing huge, but I was part of it.

Now after those nights, I feel embarrassed and wiped out, and I don’t want to be around people. I get this feeling like they’ll look at me and know I’m not holding things together the way I used to. Which is probably not true, I mean people are usually worried about their own lives—my neighbor once came to a whole meeting with two different shoes on and nobody said anything until afterward—but still, in my head it feels obvious.

So yeah, I’ve pulled back. I’ll make excuses or just not go. With family or friends, I don’t know if I can point to one big thing, but the avoiding, the not showing up… that’s definitely there.
Do you feel like your nighttime eating has affected how you see yourself or caused problems in your personal relationships, even if it's not something you've talked about directly?

Yeah… it has. I mean, I haven’t really sat people down and said, “This is what’s going on,” but it changes how I act around them.

I’ve pulled back from those community planning meetings and helping with events, which used to be something I actually liked doing. After those nights I just feel embarrassed and drained, like I don’t want anyone looking too closely at me. It’s weird, because I know nobody’s probably thinking about me that much—people are busy worrying about parking permits and folding chairs and who forgot the sign-in sheet—but in my head it feels like they’ll notice I’m not holding things together like I used to.

So I just… don’t go sometimes. Or I make excuses. And then I feel worse about that too.
Have you found that things you used to enjoy, like hobbies or activities, just don’t feel as good or interesting to you anymore?

I’m not sure. I mean… I don’t know if things don’t feel good anymore, or if I just don’t get around to them the way I used to.

Like, I’ll think about doing something, and then the day sort of gets away from me. Or I’ll sit down and there’s a rerun on TV, and then I remember this one actor was in something my mother used to watch—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I haven’t really noticed it as a clear thing, like “I don’t enjoy anything now.” It’s more hard for me to tell what’s lack of interest and what’s just me not following through.
Have you noticed that things you used to really enjoy, like hobbies or activities, don’t feel as rewarding or interesting to you anymore—even if you still do them sometimes?

I’m not really sure, honestly. I’m having trouble separating whether the things themselves feel less rewarding, or if I just… don’t make the effort to do them.

Like sometimes I’ll still watch something or think about doing an activity, and it’s okay, but then I get distracted or I don’t follow through. And then I start thinking about, I don’t know, how I used to be better at keeping a routine—like even stupid little routines, watering a plant on the same day or remembering when the recycling goes out. Not that that’s a hobby, obviously.

So… I don’t know that I can say they don’t feel interesting anymore. I haven’t noticed it that clearly. It’s more muddled than that for me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences eating episodes in the night that occur while partially awake or in a dissociated state, which could suggest Nocturnal Eating Syndrome or a parasomnia-related eating disorder.
doctor.question: When you’re eating at night, do you ever feel like you’re only partly awake, or like you’re on autopilot, not fully in control of what you’re doing?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take that first bite, it feels like the decision has already been made for me, and even while I’m telling myself, 'George, stop now,' my hands keep fixing another plate or opening another container.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the nighttime eating feels automatic or not fully under control, which most directly matches the loss of control during eating episodes.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d say I’m half-asleep exactly. It’s more like… once I take that first bite, something clicks over, and then it feels like the decision’s already been made for me.

I can be standing there thinking, George, stop. Just stop now. And meanwhile my hands are still doing it—fixing another plate, opening another container, putting something else together like I’m just following instructions. It’s a strange feeling.

It reminds me of when you drive somewhere familiar and realize you don’t remember half the turns you made—not that it’s the same thing, but that kind of autopilot. Except with this, I’m aware enough to feel ashamed while it’s happening, which makes it worse.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences distress or impairment in other areas beyond social and community activities, such as in personal relationships or self-care, related to the nighttime eating.
doctor.question: Has your nighttime eating caused any problems in your personal relationships, or do you find yourself avoiding certain situations with your family or friends because of it?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve pulled back from community planning meetings and helping with events because I feel embarrassed, drained, and afraid people will notice I’m not holding things together the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether the nighttime eating causes interpersonal or social avoidance problems, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I guess it’s less with family directly and more that I’ve started avoiding people in general, especially the community planning stuff. Like, I used to show up and help with events, make calls, organize little things—nothing huge, but I was part of it.

Now after those nights, I feel embarrassed and wiped out, and I don’t want to be around people. I get this feeling like they’ll look at me and know I’m not holding things together the way I used to. Which is probably not true, I mean people are usually worried about their own lives—my neighbor once came to a whole meeting with two different shoes on and nobody said anything until afterward—but still, in my head it feels obvious.

So yeah, I’ve pulled back. I’ll make excuses or just not go. With family or friends, I don’t know if I can point to one big thing, but the avoiding, the not showing up… that’s definitely there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in areas of functioning outside of social/community activities, such as in personal relationships or self-image, specifically related to the nighttime eating.
doctor.question: Do you feel like your nighttime eating has affected how you see yourself or caused problems in your personal relationships, even if it's not something you've talked about directly?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve pulled back from community planning meetings and helping with events because I feel embarrassed, drained, and afraid people will notice I’m not holding things together the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether the nighttime eating has caused interpersonal or social problems, which is best matched by the functional impairment item about pulling back from community meetings and avoiding people because of embarrassment and feeling drained.

patient.answer:
Yeah… it has. I mean, I haven’t really sat people down and said, “This is what’s going on,” but it changes how I act around them.

I’ve pulled back from those community planning meetings and helping with events, which used to be something I actually liked doing. After those nights I just feel embarrassed and drained, like I don’t want anyone looking too closely at me. It’s weird, because I know nobody’s probably thinking about me that much—people are busy worrying about parking permits and folding chairs and who forgot the sign-in sheet—but in my head it feels like they’ll notice I’m not holding things together like I used to.

So I just… don’t go sometimes. Or I make excuses. And then I feel worse about that too.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a lack of pleasure or interest in activities they previously found enjoyable, beyond social or community events, to assess for anhedonia as a symptom of depression.
doctor.question: Have you found that things you used to enjoy, like hobbies or activities, just don’t feel as good or interesting to you anymore?

target_item.reason: The question is about loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities, which is not covered by the provided binge-eating symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean… I don’t know if things don’t feel good anymore, or if I just don’t get around to them the way I used to.

Like, I’ll think about doing something, and then the day sort of gets away from me. Or I’ll sit down and there’s a rerun on TV, and then I remember this one actor was in something my mother used to watch—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I haven’t really noticed it as a clear thing, like “I don’t enjoy anything now.” It’s more hard for me to tell what’s lack of interest and what’s just me not following through.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient experiences a loss of pleasure or interest in activities they previously enjoyed, which would help differentiate between the remaining diagnostic candidates.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that things you used to really enjoy, like hobbies or activities, don’t feel as rewarding or interesting to you anymore—even if you still do them sometimes?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about loss of interest or reduced pleasure in hobbies/activities, which is not covered by the provided binge-eating symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure, honestly. I’m having trouble separating whether the things themselves feel less rewarding, or if I just… don’t make the effort to do them.

Like sometimes I’ll still watch something or think about doing an activity, and it’s okay, but then I get distracted or I don’t follow through. And then I start thinking about, I don’t know, how I used to be better at keeping a routine—like even stupid little routines, watering a plant on the same day or remembering when the recycling goes out. Not that that’s a hobby, obviously.

So… I don’t know that I can say they don’t feel interesting anymore. I haven’t noticed it that clearly. It’s more muddled than that for me.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for Night Eating Syndrome (F50.81) with significant distress and impairment related to nighttime overeating, lack of control during episodes, and associated shame and guilt. There is insufficient evidence for a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9) as depressed mood is not consistently present for most of the day, nor is there a clear loss of interest or pleasure in activities.
